subject: feat[dotfiles][emacs/org]: stamp Planning Inventory entries with creation time
message:
feat[dotfiles][emacs/org]: stamp Planning Inventory entries with creation time

[PROBLEM]
Planning Inventory entries (OUTCOME/TASK/NEXT-STEP/STEP in
org/kaizen/projects.org) were only ever timestamped at the *end* of their
life -- org's CLOSED: stamp on completion. Their moment of *birth* went
unrecorded, so there was no way to see when an entry entered the plan, and
therefore no way to reconstruct how the project's scope evolved over time
(entropy of expertise, scope creep, and the like).

[CAUSE]
These entries are born from yasnippets, and those snippets inserted only the
heading -- no creation stamp. A creation timestamp had never been part of the
template. Compounding this, the two sibling snippets that *did* intend to
stamp creation time (clarified-task, eod-offloading) called
`inactive-timestamp-now', but that helper was never defined anywhere in the
loaded config -- only `inactive-timestamp' (in ai/packages.el) existed -- so
the intended stamp was a latent void-function.

[SOLUTION]
Each Planning Inventory snippet now stamps the entry on expansion with an
inactive `:CAPTURE_TIME:` property drawer, e.g.

    *** OUTCOME ... [/]
    :PROPERTIES:
    :CAPTURE_TIME: [2026-07-01 Wed 12:34]
    :END:

Two deliberate choices keep this idiomatic and cohesive rather than novel:

  - Inactive timestamp (bracketed), not active (angled): a creation time is a
    fact to be queried, not an event that should surface in the agenda as if
    it were scheduled. This mirrors org's own CLOSED: stamp.
  - The existing `:CAPTURE_TIME:` property, not a new `:CREATED:`. The repo
    already records "when this came into being" as CAPTURE_TIME on roam nodes,
    cognition captures, and the clarified-task snippet. Reusing it means a TASK
    born from the `task` snippet and one born from `clarified-task` share one
    queryable field, so scope-evolution analysis reads a single property.

The phantom `inactive-timestamp-now' is made real -- defined in the ai layer's
funcs.el, which (unlike packages.el) is free of load-time side effects, so the
snippet helper stays lightweight and unit-testable. Defining it also un-breaks
clarified-task and eod-offloading for free. An ERT suite pins the two contracts
that matter: the helper yields a canonical, inactive, genuinely-parseable org
timestamp; and every Planning Inventory snippet actually embeds it, so the
requirement cannot silently regress.

refactor[dotfiles][emacs/org]: stamp creation time via the existing inactive-timestamp

[PROBLEM]
The first cut of this change reified `inactive-timestamp-now' in ai/funcs.el,
duplicating the exact algorithm of the pre-existing `inactive-timestamp'
(ai/packages.el:1392) -- both `(format-time-string "[%Y-%m-%d %a %H:%M]" ...)'.
That is Connascence of Algorithm across two files (the format dialect must now
agree in two places) and non-requisite variety (a second helper adding no
variation over the first), scattering the single "inactive timestamp" concept.

[CAUSE]
`inactive-timestamp-now' was only ever a mistyped reference living in two
snippets (clarified-task, eod-offloading); it was never defined. But
`inactive-timestamp' already covers the need: its `timestamp' argument is
optional and `format-time-string' reads "now" when it is nil, so
`(inactive-timestamp)' *is* the current-moment stamp -- and the codebase
already calls it exactly that way (ai/packages.el:3597, :3839). Reifying the
mistyped name added the duplication instead of removing it.

[SOLUTION]
Delete `inactive-timestamp-now' and route every creation stamp through the one
existing `inactive-timestamp'. All six snippets that stamp creation time now
call `(inactive-timestamp)': the four Planning Inventory snippets (OUTCOME/TASK/
NEXT-STEP/STEP) and the two callers that previously reached for the mistyped
name (clarified-task, eod-offloading), which are thereby fixed to hit the real
function rather than a void one. ai/funcs.el returns to untouched, so the format
dialect and the current-time default live in a single source.

The test suite is retargeted to the snippet-level contract it can verify without
loading the heavyweight packages.el: every Planning Inventory snippet embeds an
inactive CAPTURE_TIME computed by `inactive-timestamp', and none reaches for the
redundant `inactive-timestamp-now' (so the duplicate name cannot creep back).

subject: feat[emacs][agenda]: rebind fast journal capture from "J" to "x"
message:
feat[emacs][agenda]: rebind fast journal capture from "J" to "x"

[PROBLEM]
The standard journal capture ("j") and the quick, timer-driven capture
("J") differ only by the shift key. Reaching for one and landing on the
other is easy, so the wrong template fires and its clock semantics (the
fast one clocks into the entry and later resumes the prior clock) surprise
the user mid-capture.

[CAUSE]
Adjacent keys carried adjacent meanings. Binding two conceptually opposite
captures to "j"/"J" made them a single fat-finger apart, coupling the
selection to shift-key precision rather than to intent.

[SOLUTION]
Move the fast capture off the shift-adjacent slot to the physically
distinct "x", leaving the standard capture on "j". The value "x" is the
selector used by the capture template plist key and by both lifecycle
hooks (`agenda/fast-journal-init` and `agenda/fast-journal-cleanup`), so
all three references move together to keep the timer/clock behavior gated
on the fast template alone. "x" is unused among active capture templates
(the org-agenda "x" command lives in a separate namespace), so no
collision is introduced.

refactor[emacs][agenda]: reify fast journal capture key as a defvar

[PROBLEM]
The fast journal capture's selector key existed only as the string
literal "x" repeated in three places: the `org-capture-templates'
registration and the guards of `agenda/fast-journal-init' and
`agenda/fast-journal-cleanup'. Rebinding it therefore required three
synchronized edits — the homomorphism test failing, since a one-concept
change ("the fast capture uses a different key") did not map to a single
site.

[CAUSE]
Connascence of Value (implementation-principles.md §5.2) with degree 3:
the three sites had to agree on the same magic string, coordinated only
by convention. Nothing named the concept "the fast capture's key", so
the agreement lived implicitly across the file.

[SOLUTION]
Consolidate the value into a single unit, per the connascence table's
prescribed direction for Value (§5.2) and mirroring the in-repo
precedent cc08c7b ("reify the llm-usage directory as a defvar"). Introduce
`agenda/fast-journal-capture-key' as a top-level defvar — matching that
precedent's choice of defvar (user-overridable), naming, placement
before its users, and concise docstring. The template registration
splices it via backquote; both guards compare against it. Rebinding the
fast capture is now a one-line change at the defvar, and the timer/clock
behavior stays gated on that one selector.

Behavior-preserving: the key value is unchanged ("x"). Kept as a separate
commit from the j/J→j/x rebind so the structural change stays bisectable
(CIA-7.5).

message:
feat[emacs][cognition]: accumulate comment captures into one feedback subheading

[PROBLEM]
Capturing N observations about one cognition output cost N cumbersome
round-trips plus hand-typed structure. Each `c` press prompted for a
comment and immediately wrote a standalone block flat under the
invocation heading, so the reviewer had to hand-type a "feedback"
subheading with its tag and properties to keep the notes grouped.

[CAUSE]
The code had no representation of "the feedback for this output." A
capture was a single write-through action; the grouping boundary lived
only in the reviewer's head and hand. The solution structure was not
homomorphic to the problem, whose natural unit is a batch of comments
about one response.

[CHANGE]
Reify that batch. A buffer-local accumulator collects rendered comment
blocks across captures without touching disk; finalize writes them
together under the output's feedback subheading, reusing the shared
`cognition/--render-feedback-subtree`. Because the feedback for an output
is a single accreting entity, finalize extends an existing :FEEDBACK:
child when present rather than adding a sibling. `c` accumulates (excerpt
optional, so a note about the whole answer needs no selection); `C`
finalizes. CAPTURE_TIME uses the corpus-standard `inactive-timestamp`
form. The old write-per-comment path and its helper are removed. Result:
N captures on one output require zero manual heading or structure typing.

subject: fix[emacs][ispell]: take word lookup off the typing path, wire $WORDLIST
message:
fix[emacs][ispell]: take word lookup off the typing path, wire $WORDLIST

[PROBLEM]
Typing in any prose buffer (org journal, plain text) spams "Corfu detected
an error: ... ispell-lookup-words: No plain word-list found at system
default locations" on every corfu-auto idle cycle.  The 2025-05-25 hack
(ispell-program-name = "echo") did not stop the error and broke flyspell
in the same buffers.

[CAUSE]
Emacs 30's text-mode registers ispell-completion-at-point in every
text-mode-derived buffer (text-mode-ispell-word-completion defaults to
completion-at-point; text-mode.el:155).  The capf eagerly calls
ispell-lookup-words, which signals when no plain word-list file exists
(ispell.el:2555).  ispell discovers that file by probing FHS paths only
(/usr/share/dict/words ...; ispell.el:208); NixOS has none of them, and
the word list the system does ship (environment.wordlist.enable in
nixos/shared/common.nix, SCOWL via $WORDLIST) is never probed.  The hack
could not work because word lookup greps the word-list file directly and
never launches ispell-program-name; pointing the program at "echo" only
disabled the real spell checker that flyspell (enabled by
technical-writing in these same buffers) depends on.

[CHANGE]
Add a technical-writing-local ispell-wordlist module owning one policy:
(1) setopt text-mode-ispell-word-completion nil -- dictionary popups per
idle cycle are noise and an eager synchronous subprocess each; upstream
corfu recommends disabling; (2) once ispell loads, point
ispell-alternate-dictionary at a readable $WORDLIST so deliberate lookups
(M-x ispell-complete-word) serve the system word list; machines without
$WORDLIST keep stock probing.  dotspacemacs/user-init calls the module
early, mirroring the lsp-booster pattern, because text-mode reads the
option once at mode activation; $WORDLIST resolution stays deferred to
ispell load time because Spacemacs imports the session environment after
user-init.  Remove the "echo" hack from coding/init-corfu, restoring
spell-checker discovery (aspell ships system-wide via common.nix).

Alternatives considered: wiring $WORDLIST alone would silence the error
but leave dictionary popups on every keystroke idle in prose; keeping the
policy as a .spacemacs defun (first iteration) left it unreachable by
run-tests.sh, so the layer-local module gives it a testable home with
four outcome-level expectations (prose completion registers no ispell
capf and never signals; $WORDLIST feeds deliberate lookup; absent or
unreadable $WORDLIST preserves stock discovery).

subject: fix[emacs][agenda]: restore the interrupted clock when a capture is cancelled
message:
fix[emacs][agenda]: restore the interrupted clock when a capture is cancelled

[PROBLEM]
Cancelling a clock-borrowing capture (:clock-in t :clock-keep nil
:resume-clock t -- Fast Journal, Friction, Break) does not restore the
clock state the capture interrupted.  The previously clocked entry's
segment stays closed at the capture-start time, and the hand-back merely
opens a new segment at cancel time: the minutes between capture start
and cancel vanish from every record, and the logbook permanently shows
an interruption whose cause -- the aborted capture entry -- org already
discarded.  Cancel should leave the clock as if it was never clocked
out.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
agenda/capture-lifecycle-cleanup runs on org-capture-after-finalize-hook
for filing and cancelling alike, but treats both as filing: it hands the
clock back with a plain org-clock-in, which always opens a new segment
from now.  That is right when the capture is filed -- the filed entry
keeps the interval it clocked, so the interrupted entry must not reclaim
it -- and wrong on cancel, where org deletes the capture entry together
with its clock segment: the interruption must be undone, not merely
followed by a fresh segment.  A comment in agenda/capture-lifecycle-init
entrenched the gap by claiming the after-finalize hook does not run on
abort; in fact org-capture-kill suppresses only the before-finalize
hook, so cleanup does run on abort and can tell the two paths apart
through org-note-abort.

[CHANGE]
On the shape the preceding refactor prepared: save the interrupted
clock's segment start time alongside its marker; on org-note-abort,
reopen the exact segment the capture's clock-in closed -- strip the
"--[end] => duration" suffix org-clock-out appended -- and clock back
in with org-clock-in-resume bound, so org adopts the reopened line:
original start time, correct mode-line total, no extra segment.  The
filed path is unchanged.  Reusing org's resume machinery beats
hand-rolling clock state (which would duplicate org internals) and
beats deleting the line to re-clock-in with a start-time argument (a
missed line match would then double-count the closed segment; the
reopen approach instead degrades to the old fresh-segment behavior).

The mocked capture-lifecycle tests that covered the clock path asserted
mock-call mechanics and kept passing while the real behavior was broken;
capture-resume-clock-test.el replaces them, driving real org-capture end
to end.  It specifies cancel-restore, filing hand-back, the no-clock and
non-borrowing-template guards through both the file and cancel paths,
and the degradation guarantee that a vanished segment yields a fresh
segment rather than a revived or double-counted one.

subject: fix[emacs][agenda]: wire org-capture-extras from its own init
message:
fix[emacs][agenda]: wire org-capture-extras from its own init

[PROBLEM]
Startup broke with "org-capture/:config: Symbol's function definition
is void: agenda/configure-capture-ux": org-capture's whole use-package
:config aborts when org-capture-extras is not the file that actually
got loaded -- a symlink farm that predates the new local package
directory, or a shadowing org-capture-extras.el earlier on load-path,
leaves the feature name resolvable while our definitions are absent.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The extraction commit wired the module from the wrong side: org-capture's
post-init called module functions directly, making org-capture's
configuration hard-depend on the module having loaded correctly.  Its
guard, (require 'org-capture-extras), cannot detect a stale or shadowed
module -- the feature still resolves -- and the comment justifying it
misread Spacemacs's configure order: configuration-layer//configure-
packages-2 runs ALL init functions before ALL post-init functions, so
the module's init normally loads it before any post-init and the require
was dead weight on the healthy path while masking nothing on the broken
one.

[CHANGE]
Wire the module from its own side: agenda/init-org-capture-extras
declares :after org-capture and installs the advices in its :config, so
activation travels with the module; org-capture's post-init keeps only
the layer's policy (agenda/configure-journal), which references the
module by symbol alone.  A missing or shadowed module now degrades to
use-package's "Cannot load org-capture-extras" warning -- naming the
real problem -- while journal templates and lifecycle hook wiring still

message:
fix[emacs][tmrts]: declare frame display parameters so themed frame creation cannot cycle

[PROBLEM]
Typing in a magit COMMIT_EDITMSG buffer spams a corfu error on every
keystroke in the doom-themed instances:

    Corfu detected an error:
      (error "Face inheritance results in inheritance cycle" gnus-group-news-low)

Corfu creates a child frame per completion popup, so no completion
popup ever appears -- corfu looks entirely broken -- and any other
frame creation ("M-m F n") dies the same way.  This is the successor
of the error 228f402 fixed: that commit eliminated the CROSS-theme
cycle from stacked themes, which unmasked this SINGLE-theme one.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
Emacs >= 31 rejects face-inheritance cycles inside `set-face-attribute'.
`x-create-frame-with-faces' recalculates every face on the new frame
BEFORE `frame-set-background-mode' computes the frame's `display-type'
and `background-mode' parameters (faces.el), yet `(class color)' /
`(background dark)' spec conditions match against exactly those
parameters.  During that early pass every display-conditioned theme
spec fails to match and the face falls back to its defface, while
unconditional `t' specs still apply.

Doom themes redirect gnus faces in the opposite direction of stock
gnus.el, split across those two spec shapes (doom-themes-base.el):

    stock gnus.el:  gnus-group-news-low        :inherit gnus-group-news-low-empty
    doom (t spec):  gnus-group-news-low-empty  :inherit gnus-group-news-low
    doom (class-conditioned):  gnus-group-news-low  :inherit gnus-group-mail-1

The finished state is acyclic, but the early pass applies the defface
for -low (conditioned spec unmatched) and doom's inversion for
-low-empty (t spec) -- the pair transiently closes on itself, the
cycle check aborts the frame, and corfu retries on the next keystroke.
Once gnus.el is loaded (message/org-mime pull it in), every frame
creation in a doom-themed instance fails.  Upstream is aware and
untriaged: doomemacs/themes#883.

[CHANGE]
Declare the display facts of this setup -- color displays, dark
backgrounds -- in `default-frame-alist' (tmrts layer config.el).
Frames are then born with the parameters the early pass reads, so
display-conditioned theme specs match from the first recalculation and
no transient defface/theme mix can arise, for any face pair in any
theme.  `frame-set-background-mode' recomputes both parameters right
after, so the declaration only covers the birth window.

Alternatives considered:
- Patch doom's gnus specs after load-theme: fixes one face pair; any
  other conditioned-vs-unconditional inversion reintroduces the class
  (exactly how this error succeeded the org-headline-done one).
- Wait for doom-themes upstream: #883 is open and untriaged.
- Suppress corfu's error reporting: masks the failure; "M-m F n" and
  every other frame creation still die.

Verified end-to-end under Xvfb against the real doom-pine + gnus.el +
corfu (throwaway ERT scaffolding, not committed): without the
declaration a control recalc reproduces the exact cycle and the corfu
popup frame dies with the reported backtrace reaching *Messages*; with
it, typing pops a live, visible corfu child frame, the gnus faces land
theme-intended, and *Messages* stays clean.

message:
refactor[dotfiles][emacs/ai]: derive the cognition keymap from one binding table

[PROBLEM]
What a cognition key is *for* had nowhere to live.  The keymap recorded
which command each key runs; the purpose that makes a key worth pressing,
and the concern it belongs to, sat in comments beside four of the thirteen
bindings and nowhere for the rest.  No code could read those comments, so
nothing could tell the reader what the mode offers.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
`define-minor-mode' built the keymap inline, one `define-key' call per
binding.  `define-key' carries exactly two facts -- key and command -- so
the rest had no home but a comment.

[CHANGE]
Name the concept: `cognition/mode-bindings' holds (HEADING ROWS) groups of
(KEY COMMAND LABEL) rows, and `cognition-mode-map' is derived from it, so
a key, its command, its purpose and its heading stay one fact in one
place.  Grouping is data rather than commentary because it is the
structure a reader scans by, and it mirrors the section-and-heads shape of
this layer's other key listings (`cognition/actions', `lsp/actions',
`cognition/trace-tags'), leaving the table convertible to one.

Two details earn their weight.  The bindings install from a top-level call
rather than a `defvar' initializer, because the table is a `defconst' that
re-evaluates on load while a `defvar' initializer does not: deriving the
keymap there would leave an edited table unreachable in a reloaded session
until Emacs restarted.  And the install mutates the keymap instead of
replacing it, because `minor-mode-map-alist' holds the keymap *object* --
a buffer already in `cognition-mode' keeps whatever object it was handed,
so re-assigning the variable would strand it on the old bindings.

Behaviour is unchanged: the derived map binds the same thirteen keys to
the same commands as the inline form it replaces, checked by building both
and comparing them key by key.

Alternative considered: keep the inline keymap and add a parallel list of
labels -- rejected, because two lists kept in the same order by convention
drift apart the first time a binding moves.

Asking a cognition response buffer "which keys do I have here?" cost the
reader their window layout.  "?" opened *Help* over a visible buffer,
where the mode's dozen keys sat buried in pages of major-mode
documentation: switch to the window, search it, quit it, then restore the
buffer it displaced -- four steps to answer a question worth one
keystroke.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
`cognition-mode' bound no "?", so the key fell through to the major mode.
Cognition buffers run `gfm-view-mode', which inherits `markdown-view-mode's
map, and that map binds "?" to `describe-mode'.  The mode had no answer of
its own, so the major mode's answer -- about the major mode -- is what
arrived.

[CHANGE]
Bind "?" to `cognition/show-bindings', which echoes the bindings table a
heading at a time, wrapped to the frame:

  Help   ? this list
  Files  f trace   ` prompt
  Notes  c comment   C finalize   L label trace
  Rerun  o optimize prompt   R replay
  Yank   y as feedback   Y id   K region as org
  Buffer U rename   q bury   Q kill

A minor-mode map shadows the major mode's, so the binding both supplies
the missing answer and displaces `describe-mode' (still on C-h m for the
full description).

The echo area is what makes the answer free: it costs no window, displaces
no buffer, and clears itself on the next keystroke.  Three alternatives
were rejected for failing exactly that.  A dedicated help buffer repeats
the problem in smaller form.  `which-key' still opens and manages a side
window, and lists raw command names rather than what they do.  A hydra --
the mechanism this layer already uses for key menus -- renders through
`lv' by default, which splits a window; per-hydra `:verbosity 1' does
route the hint to the echo area, but the display would then hinge on a
property whose loss fails silently, back to splitting a window.

The listing is derived, not written: it reads the same table the keymap
does, so a key added there is documented under its heading without a
second edit.

subject: refactor[dotfiles][emacs/roam]: derive ID prefixes from the entry's file, not its buffer name
message:
refactor[dotfiles][emacs/roam]: derive ID prefixes from the entry's file, not its buffer name

[PROBLEM]
Declaring "entries in this file get this ID prefix" took a regex that
also had to encode org-capture's buffer-naming convention:

    "\\`\\(?:CAPTURE-.*\\)?journal\\.org\\'"

One fact -- journal entries are prefixed `journal:' -- stated as a
buffer-name pattern plus the shape of the name org gives a capture
buffer.  Every further file would restate that shape, and each
restatement is a chance to get it wrong: this one already misses
capture-journal.org when the file is visited directly rather than
captured into.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The rules asked the wrong question.  An entry's kind depends on the
file it belongs to, but the code inspected the buffer it is displayed
in -- and during a capture those differ, because org edits the entry in
an indirect buffer named after the target file.  Buffer names are org's
business; reading them made every rule restate org's convention.

[CHANGE]
Ask which file the entry belongs to.  `roam/-entry-file' answers it
once -- via the base buffer, so a capture buffer resolves to its target
-- and both the ID's location registration and its prefix now derive
from that one answer.

With files as the question, the rules become data: two alists, keyed by
file name and by TODO state, replacing the regex and the cond chain.
Adding a prefix is now adding a row, and no row mentions capture.
The alternative -- keeping regexes but generating the CAPTURE- variant
-- was rejected: it still leaks a convention that is not ours to model.

Asking the right question also closes the gap named above: an entry
visited directly in capture-journal.org now gets `journal:' instead of
falling through to the prefix prompt.  Every other outcome is
unchanged, the heading's state still outranking the file it sits in.

The nested `defun's the rules lived in are lifted to top level, which
retires the `declare-function' stanza that existed only to hide them
from the byte-compiler.

feat[dotfiles][emacs/kaizen]: let popper manage forge post buffers

[PROBLEM]
Calling `forge-create-post' to comment on an issue or pull-request
splits whatever window layout is on screen, and the composition buffer
stays there until the post is submitted or cancelled.  Every other
buffer that arrives this way -- claude, aidermacs, shell output -- is a
popper popup instead: a right side window, dismissable with `w;'.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
`popper-reference-buffers' never named it.  Popper takes over a
buffer's display only when `popper-popup-p' matches it, so an unlisted
buffer falls through to plain `display-buffer' -- which splits.

[CHANGE]
Add `forge-post-mode' to the list.

Matched by mode, where every existing entry is a name regexp, because
forge builds these buffers with `find-file-noselect' over a draft file
under .git/magit/posts/: the buffer name is that file's name
("42;new-comment"), which uniquify decorates further once two
repositories hold a draft of the same name.  That naming is private to
`forge--post-expand-file-name', so matching on it would couple this
configuration to an internal we do not own.  The major mode is forge's
public surface, and `forge--setup-post-buffer' sets it on the buffer
itself.

The rule therefore covers every forge post buffer, not just
`forge-create-post': new issue, new pull-request, edit post and topic
note all compose in `forge-post-mode' and all disrupt the layout
identically.  Singling out create-post would need exactly the file-name
matching rejected above.

No test accompanies this.  The rule's contract is popper's own
documented matching of `popper-reference-buffers' entries; asserting the
list contains the entry would restate the configuration and nothing
more -- the tautological gate this repository deleted in e78f65b.  What
did need checking is that popper's classifier buckets the symbol as a
major mode rather than a predicate while forge is still unloaded, since
`popper-mode' activates long before the deferred forge package loads;
it does, on the "-mode" suffix.

message:
fix[dotfiles][xmonad]: disable enabled themes before theming dedicated Emacs instances

[PROBLEM]
Typing in the `externalized-cognition` instance (e.g. a magit
COMMIT_EDITMSG buffer) spams a corfu error on every keystroke:

    Corfu detected an error:
      (error "Face inheritance results in inheritance cycle" org-headline-done)

Any frame creation in that instance trips the same error (journal,
2026-02-08: "M-m F n" fails with `face-spec-set-2: Face inheritance
results in inheritance cycle: org-headline-done`); corfu is merely the
loudest trigger because it creates a child frame per completion popup.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The dedicated-instance spawn commands switch themes with a bare
`load-theme`, which stacks themes instead of replacing them. The
startup theme (catppuccin, first entry of `dotspacemacs-themes`) stays
enabled underneath doom-pine, and `face-spec-recalc` merges BOTH
themes' face specs on every new frame. Their org faces inherit in
opposite directions:

    catppuccin: (org-headline-done :inherit org-done)
    doom:       (org-done :inherit org-headline-done ...)

Merged, the two faces inherit from each other. Newer Emacs builds (the
cycle check is absent from 30.1) reject the cycle inside
`set-face-attribute`, which runs for every face on every frame
creation — corfu popups and "M-m F n" alike. Reproduced in
`emacs --batch`: stacking the two specs yields the mutual :inherit;
disabling the first theme before loading the second does not.

[CHANGE]
`emacsInstanceCommand` now emits
`(mapc 'disable-theme custom-enabled-themes)` before `load-theme`, so
the alternate theme replaces the startup theme and no cross-theme face
merge can arise — for both existing instances (`externalized-cognition`,
`nostramo`) and any future (name, theme) pair.

Alternatives considered:
- `(disable-theme 'catppuccin)`: silently regresses the day the
  startup theme changes; disabling whatever is enabled tracks the
  config instead.
- `spacemacs/load-theme` with its DISABLE flag: the flag is only
  honoured on the fallback path (core-themes-support.el), so the happy
  path would still stack.
- Patching the face specs in one theme: fixes one symptom; any other
  theme pair with mutually inheriting faces would reintroduce the
  error.

Verified end-to-end: the generated command, executed via `sh -c`
against a real Emacs with a stand-in startup theme pre-enabled, ends
with only the alternate theme enabled.

feat[dotfiles][emacs/technical-writing]: add LLM vocabulary candidates as inline annotations

[PROBLEM]
While writing (mostly org journal entries) there is no fast way to find a
better word: synosaurus is context-blind (its search-and-replace keybinding
TODO sat unfinished), and the cognition LLM path is built for depth, not
flow -- opus with extended thinking, request structs, Langfuse logging, and
display buffers add multi-second latency and yank the writer out of the
buffer.

[CAUSE]
Both existing tools optimize for a different problem. A thesaurus cannot
rank candidates by the surrounding sentence, and the cognition pipeline's
weight is intrinsic to its job (traced, logged, reasoning-heavy requests),
so neither can be tuned into a keypress-speed, mid-writing tool; the
latency and the UI interruption are structural.

[CHANGE]
Add a self-contained `vocabulary' local package (mirroring the
agenda/attention-slot precedent): M-* annotates the word/phrase at point
with a flycheck-style overlay and fires an async request to a dedicated
minimal gptel backend -- claude-haiku, no thinking, non-streaming,
structured-outputs JSON schema, capped context centered on point -- then
renders the candidates inline at the target when they arrive (verified
end-to-end at ~1.1s). Overlays move with the text, so the writer keeps
typing and comes back to accept (M-*), retry a failure (M-*), or dismiss
(C-u M-*) whenever. A minibuffer-blocking design was rejected because it
interrupts writing; routing through the cognition pipeline was rejected
because its overhead is structural (see CAUSE). The ERT suite (30 tests)
stubs only the network and picker boundaries and asserts buffer/annotation
outcomes; the 3 failing suites in ai/agenda pre-date this change (identical
on the merge base).

message:
feat[dotfiles][emacs/technical-writing]: render candidates vertically below the target

[PROBLEM]
PR #285 request: the horizontal run-on row of candidates is hard to scan,
especially for phrase candidates; a vertical column below the word reads
at a glance.

[CAUSE]
The first cut hung all candidates off one inline after-string at the
target -- the simplest rendering, but one whose readability degrades
linearly with candidate length.

[CHANGE]
Render the candidates as a phantom block below the target's line using
the flycheck-inline overlay pattern (the established lightweight
approach): a second overlay spans the newline at end-of-line and carries
the padded, numbered lines in its after-string (newline-prefixed at
end-of-buffer, where there is no newline to span), aligned under the
target's column. The block is derived presentation: it renders and
clears only through `vocabulary--set-status', re-anchors on every
transition, and dies with its annotation on dismissal. Error text uses
the same mechanism, so there is still exactly one rendering site.
posframe/child-frame rendering was rejected as heavier than the problem
requires and worse in terminals.

feat[emacs][agenda]: add friction, break, and stimulant capture templates

[PROBLEM]
FRICTION entries, stimulant logs, and breaks recur many times a day in the
journal, but no capture template exists for them: each one is typed by
hand -- heading, tag, timestamp, dose line, clock -- restating the same
structure dozens of times a week and inviting drift between entries.

[CAUSE]
Until the journal capture catalogue existed, adding an entry type cost a
full copied template block, so recurring types never got templates and
the structure lived only in muscle memory.

[CHANGE]
Declare the three types in `agenda/journal-capture-templates', each a
single capture keystroke with structure and tag pre-filled, shaped after
the existing journal corpus:

- "f" Friction: prompted heading tagged :FRICTION:, timestamped, clocked
  in with :clock-keep -- friction entries are written while wrestling
  with the obstacle, so the time spent belongs to the entry.
- "b" Break: the recurring break activities (shower, guided/unguided
  painting, stretching) offered as completions, tagged :BREAK:, clock
  left running so clocking out on return records the break's duration.
- "s" Stimulant: substance completions (modafinil, caffeine, l-theanine)
  as the tagged heading plus a dose prompt; a point-in-time log, so no
  clock.

Keys "f", "b", "s" are unclaimed across every layer's global capture
templates.  The suite covers each type end-to-end: tag and structure of
the filed text, offered completions, and clock behavior.

the existing constructor. Friction and Break now declare only what makes

drives real org-capture, so it asserts what a user sees -- the filed
entry's tag and the clock state afterwards -- rather than the shape of a

commit in this series exists to eliminate.  When it does not recover, the
second failure escapes uncaught in place of the first.

message:
refactor[dotfiles][emacs/agenda]: move the capture lifecycle wiring into its module

[PROBLEM]
What the capture lifecycle installs is stated in three places and
reconciled by convention alone.  `agenda/configure-journal' adds the two
hooks (funcs.el), the test harness re-states them by hand, and the
harness docstring asserts the two agree -- "installed exactly as
`agenda/configure-journal' installs them" -- which nothing checks.  A
harness that drifts from the installer still compiles and still passes,
and the suite then quietly stops exercising the wiring it claims to
mirror.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The module owns the lifecycle but not its activation.  Every other piece
of org-capture-extras installs itself -- `agenda/configure-capture-ux'
does, from packages.el -- while the lifecycle hooks are wired from the
layer, which the module's own commentary declares the home of capture
POLICY: which templates exist and what they declare.  Wiring left in the
layer has no home to be single, so each caller keeps its own copy.

[CHANGE]
Give the wiring one home: `agenda/configure-capture-lifecycle', beside
the hooks it installs and mirroring `agenda/configure-capture-ux' at the
end of its own section.  packages.el activates both, one call per module
section; `agenda/configure-journal' keeps templates and nothing else,
and drops the two `declare-function' promises it no longer needs.

The harness now calls that installer instead of restating it, so the
equivalence its docstring claimed holds by construction.  The hooks stay
let-bound -- empty rather than pre-filled -- which keeps global hooks out
of the scratch world and undoes the installation on exit.

Moving activation also improves how a broken module degrades.  Wiring
from the layer, `add-hook' on a void symbol succeeds and fails later
inside a capture; from the module's own `:config', use-package warns and
installs nothing -- the degradation packages.el already documents for
this package.

Filing a clocked capture within the minute it started leaves

  CLOCK: [2026-07-26 Sun 13:23]--[2026-07-26 Sun 13:23] =>  0:00

on the captured entry, inside a LOGBOOK drawer holding nothing else.

the journal accrues clock lines that record no work.

segment measured.  `org-clock-out-remove-zero-time-clocks' is org's own
switch for suppressing the empty ones, and it defaults to nil; this
configuration never set it.

capture out.

holding the capture's own clock-out and not the interrupted entry's.
Setting the option globally, or across the whole capture, would also
reach the segment the capture closes on the interrupted entry when it
clocks itself in.  That segment is load-bearing: cancelling restores the
interrupted clock by reopening it, and even at zero duration it records
a task still in progress rather than a spent capture.

Scoping by buffer instead of by time cannot express that distinction.
`org-clock-in' anchors `org-clock-marker' in the capture buffer's BASE
buffer, and `org-clock-out' reads the option there -- so a buffer-local
value lands on the target file's buffer, which the interrupted task
shares whenever it too lives in the journal.

Advice rather than a hook because org closes the clock inside
`org-capture-finalize', between `org-capture-mode-hook' and
`org-capture-after-finalize-hook'; no seam sits at that moment.  Being
the lifecycle's first piece that outlives a `let', it also gives
`agenda/unconfigure-capture-lifecycle' its reason to exist, and the test
world its teardown.

neither clock line nor drawer, and cancelling still restores an
interrupted clock that had itself been running under a minute -- the
boundary a global setting would have crossed.

Tracking an entry popped an org-capture buffer over the work being

collected was the same word almost every time, and for a section that

which is a text cursor: the only way to put a word there was to open a
buffer around it and let the user type.  A template that asks nothing has

answer, so the window was the mechanism.

picker the destination prompt already uses, so tracking an entry is two

vertico headers so the ordering states its evidence instead of asserting
itself: what this destination has filed ("filed here"), what sections
named like it have filed ("filed in other impact sections" -- all a

becomes a suggestion next time.

refactor[dotfiles][emacs/kaizen]: file the tracker line instead of capturing it

[PROBLEM]
The command still went through org-capture to add one fully determined
line.  It built a throwaway template with an invented key, bound it as the
sole template, called `org-capture', and set :immediate-finish to stop the
window it did not want from opening -- a flag whose whole job was to
suppress the machinery being invoked.

Everything org-capture does beyond inserting text was either unwanted or a
hazard here: the template ran through %-expansion, so a heading holding
"%(" or "%[" would have been mangled on its way into the link text; the
capture lifecycle hooks fired on a capture nobody could see; and
`agenda/org-capture-elaborate' could not reach the capture anyway, which
needed a paragraph of explanation in the last commit.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
org-capture composes: it exists to open a buffer, expand a template, and
let the user write.  Once the prompts settled every fact, nothing was left
to compose -- but the write path was still the composing machine, so its
cost stayed and its behaviour had to be argued about.

[CHANGE]
Write the line.  `pos/--file-tracker-line' visits the file, finds the
destination's outline path, puts the line after the ones already filed
there, and saves.  `pos/--tracker-line' names the shape being written and
sits beside `pos/--filed-line-regexp', which reads that shape back: filing
and reading evidence are two halves of one format, and they now sit in
view of each other.

and nothing the user can see, so it emulates org-capture down to the empty
lines: `org-capture-empty-lines-before' normalised the blank line between a
section and the next heading away, and so does this.  Verified by running
both implementations over the same four fixtures -- trailing blank line, no
blank line, empty section, last section in the file -- and diffing the
files byte for byte.

Saving is kept too: `org-capture-finalize' saved the target buffer, and
nothing in this workflow comes back to save the tracker.  A test pins that
the line is on disk when the command returns, which nothing had asserted
while org-capture was doing it.

feat[dotfiles][emacs/ai]: capture and dispatch delegation requests to cloud sessions

[PROBLEM]
Sending a delegation request to a Claude cloud session means leaving
Emacs: open a terminal inside the target checkout, write the prompt
into a file, invoke the delegate-frictions skill's dispatch.sh with the
right positional arguments, then watch the transcript for the
created-session line.  That friction defeats the point of delegation --
a request should cost one keystroke and a typed thought, not a context
switch that displaces the work the request came out of.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The dispatch machinery stops at the CLI layer.  dispatch.sh owns the
hard parts -- the pseudo-TTY `claude --remote' demands outside a
terminal, the task-file convention that keeps arbitrary prose out of
shell quoting -- but nothing bridges the editor to it: no capture
surface, no carrier for the model/repository/permission-mode/effort
parameters, and no reader of the transcript verdict the skill's
dispatch reference defines.

[CHANGE]
Add an `ai' layer local package, delegate-dispatch.  The entry command
pops a 12-line capture strip at the frame bottom (also on the cognition
hydra as "D"); C-c C-c writes the request to a temp task file, runs
dispatch.sh asynchronously, and restores the windows; C-c C-k abandons.
The header line shows the knob state -- model, target repository,
permission mode, effort -- each adjustable via a C-c chord.  The
repository knob resolves to the directory the script runs in, because
`claude --remote' infers the session's repository from its cwd;
mono-repo is configured as the default target.  A process sentinel
greps the ANSI-stripped transcript for the reference's terminal states:
created-session reports success and puts the resume command on the kill
ring; an Error line -- or silence, which must never pass for success --
reports failure and keeps the transcript buffer for diagnosis.

The script stays the command of record: the package restates neither
the CLI invocation nor the effort default (no effort argument is sent
unless the user overrides it), so those facts keep their single home in
the skill.  Structure mirrors command-census -- a pure core (argv
contract, transcript parsing) reached through explicit arguments, thin
capture/process glue around it -- and personal wiring (script path,
repository list, markdown capture buffers) stays in packages.el.
Twelve ERT cases specify the behavior, two of them end-to-end against a
receipt-writing stub script; the alternative of asserting on a stubbed
`make-process' argv everywhere would have pinned mechanism, not
outcome.

[PROBLEM]
The problem names one concept -- a dispatch KNOB: a parameter with a

per-capture seeding into a single `--knob-state' alist that `--send'

nil-means-script-default) lives inside that knob's own entry.

knob is one table entry plus its candidate list; remembering last-used

subject: fix[dotfiles][emacs]: import the shell environment when no frame exists
message:
fix[dotfiles][emacs]: import the shell environment when no frame exists

[PROBLEM]
Emacs could not find git:

    custom-initialize-reset: Searching for program: No such file or directory, git
    process-file: Searching for program: No such file or directory, git [2 times]

The same startup logged the same failure for jupyter, 28 times over.  Both
binaries are installed -- `gitFull' and `jupyter' are in
`environment.systemPackages'.  Neither was reachable.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
`exec-path' never held the login shell's PATH, so `process-file' had nowhere
to look.  `dotspacemacs/user-env' called `spacemacs/load-spacemacs-env',
which imports only `(when (or force (display-graphic-p)) ...)'
(core-env.el).  This Emacs runs as a systemd user daemon -- `services.emacs'
in nixos/shared/common.nix, restarted by xmonad with `systemctl --user
restart emacs' -- and a daemon initialises before any frame exists, so the
guard read nil on every start.

The devenv dotfile carried the same call, and there the guard is not merely
usually nil but necessarily so: boot-profile.el is copied to ~/.spacemacs in
a headless container, which never has a frame to acquire.

Nothing logged the skip, which is why a year passed between the 2024-09-27
sighting of this and its diagnosis.

[CHANGE]
Pass FORCE, from one place both dotfiles call.

FORCE is the public way past the frame guard, so no private core-env symbol
is copied here -- a copy would keep working right up until upstream added a
step to `spacemacs/load-spacemacs-env', then diverge without a sound.  It
also regenerates .spacemacs.env instead of trusting what is on disk: that
file is gitignored and otherwise written exactly once, so a capture taken in
a degraded environment would stick forever.  The price is two shell spawns,
paid when a daemon boots or a container comes up.

`spacemacs-env.el' is that one place, at the layer-tree root beside
`layer-test-utils.el'.  Both dotfiles now delegate, so "how this repository
imports the shell environment" has a single home; previously the desktop and
devenv answers sat in different files, and only one of them was about to be
fixed.

Verification is the other half.  `spacemacs//init-spacemacs-env' captures by
spawning `shell-file-name' with -lc/-ic, and a systemd user unit need not
set SHELL -- so the capture can quietly come up thin without anything
raising.  `tmrts/import-shell-environment' therefore probes `exec-path' for
git afterwards and warns at :error when it is absent, naming `C-u M-x
spacemacs/load-spacemacs-env' as the recovery.  Not
`spacemacs/force-init-spacemacs-env', which is `(spacemacs//init-spacemacs-env
t)' and nothing else: it rewrites the file without loading it, leaving the
running session unchanged, and upstream's keybinding says as much --
"Recreate env. variables file".

git is the whole canary set on purpose.  It is what magit, forge, projectile
and vc all shell out to, and what failed here; a longer list would cry wolf
on a machine missing some optional tool.

The suite pins the predicate, not the plumbing: a truncated `exec-path'
names what cannot be launched, a repaired one reports nothing.  Driving the
import itself would need Spacemacs core and live login shells, and the only
assertion left over -- "user-env calls load-env-vars" -- would restate the
configuration rather than test it.

refactor[dotfiles][emacs]: let the import own exec-path

[PROBLEM]
Answering "what is on `exec-path'?" meant reading three things in two files:
the import in `dotspacemacs/user-env', a live PATH-building block in
`dotspacemacs/user-config', and a commented-out PATH snapshot above it.

The comment had gone stale in a way that actively misled.  Its
NOTE(2024-09-27) records the same jupyter incident the preceding fix
re-diagnoses from scratch, and attributes it to PATH holding "%s" -- so the
file offered two accounts of one event, neither citing the other, the older
contradicting the newer.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The block predates a working import.  While `dotspacemacs/user-env' silently
did nothing, appending $GOBIN and $CARGOBIN by hand was the only thing
putting them within reach, and hardcoding PATH outright was a reasonable
last resort.  Repairing the import made both redundant without removing
either.

Redundant, and in one case wrong: bash/.bashrc.env:31-34 exports GOPATH as
"$HOME/golang/" and GOBIN as "$GOPATH/bin", yielding "$HOME/golang//bin",
while this file built "$HOME/golang/bin".  `add-to-list' compares with
`equal', so the two spellings of one directory both landed on `exec-path'.
The commented snapshot is the evidence -- it shows the shell's doubled
slash.

[CHANGE]
Delete the dead snapshot and its note, and stop writing PATH and `exec-path'
here.  The login shell already exports all three directories, and the import
now actually reads it, so `exec-path' has exactly one source.

$GOPATH, $GOBIN, $CARGOBIN and $SOLC stay as plain variables: Go and Rust
tooling read them directly rather than through PATH, and $SOLC has no other
home -- no shell dotfile exports it.  Keeping them costs nothing and does
not reopen the question this commit closes, because a variable is not a
search path.

Dropping them was the alternative, on the grounds that .bashrc.env exports
the other three.  Rejected: only the interactive capture pass sources that
file, so a login-shell-only capture would lose them silently.  Should the
import ever come up that thin, git goes missing with them and the canary
added in the preceding commit says so.

subject: feat[dotfiles][emacs/ai]: align the cognition listing into a grid
message:
feat[dotfiles][emacs/ai]: align the cognition listing into a grid

[PROBLEM]
Entries began wherever the previous label ended, so the keys sat at six
different columns and the eye had no line to follow down the listing.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The renderer placed each entry immediately after the last, with a fixed
separator between them.  There was no notion of a column shared between
the groups, so nothing could line up.

[CHANGE]
Lay out, then render.  `cognition/--layout-bindings' breaks each group's
entries into lines that fit the frame; `cognition/--slot-widths' measures
what actually landed in each slot; the renderer pads to those columns:

  Help   ? this list
  Files  f trace             ` prompt
  Notes  c comment           C finalize   L label trace
  Rerun  o optimize prompt   R replay
  Yank   y as feedback       Y id         K region as org
  Buffer U rename            q bury       Q kill

Splitting the two is what makes the grid survive a wrap.  Slot widths are
keyed on where an entry was placed, not on its index within its group --
those coincide only until a group wraps, and then a continuation line's
entries are padded for columns they do not occupy.  With a group of four
Files keys at 55 columns, the old code put the continuation's second
entry at screen column 31 against a grid column of 27; it now lands on
the grid.

Padding also only ever goes *before* an entry, so an entry is charged for
what it occupies rather than for a column it is about to have trimmed off
its end.  The old fit test measured padding it then stripped, wrapping
lines that fit: at 53 columns the listing ran to nine lines where six
would have done.

Two costs, both deliberate.  Slots are sized before we know what lands in
them, so the fit test is conservative and the listing reaches six lines
at 62 columns rather than 55 -- an iterative fixed point would recover
those seven columns and is not worth a solver for a fourteen-row menu.
And no line may overflow, which is provable rather than tested by
example: rendering places every entry at or left of where the fit test
measured it.  Checked across widths 12 to 120 -- no line exceeds its
width above 23 columns (below that the heading plus the widest entry
cannot fit at all, and an over-long line beats a listing missing a key),
and no key is ever dropped.

subject: feat[dotfiles][emacs/agenda]: relocate the day's staged captures into the journal
message:
feat[dotfiles][emacs/agenda]: relocate the day's staged captures into the journal

[PROBLEM]
Journal captures never reach the journal on their own.  They are staged
in the capture journal so org-capture stays instant and so the day's
stimulants, breaks and frictions stay out of the journal while the day
runs -- but moving them across afterwards is hand work: cut each entry,
find its day in a five-megabyte datetree, and drop it at the right point
in the day's chronology.  Doing that dozens of times a day is enough
friction to leave entries stranded.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
Only half the workflow was ever built.  Capture had a home in the layer;
filing had none, so it fell to whoever was at the keyboard.

[CHANGE]
Add `agenda/journal-relocate-captures', bound to M-j m, and give it the
journal-relocate local package to live in.  It takes every day that is
over, files each entry under that day in the journal, and leaves the
capture journal as small as it started -- emptied year, month and day
scaffolding included.  Today stays staged, because the day is still in
progress; a prefix argument takes it too, for wrapping the day up.

Two facts drive the design.  Staged entries are not chronological --
captures are appended as they finalize, so an entry begun at 10:46 and
finished at 11:20 sits below one captured whole at 11:18 -- so the
command orders them by each entry's own %U timestamp, read through org's
TIMESTAMP_IA, which looks past a LOGBOOK drawer and never mistakes a
sub-entry's stamp for its parent's.  And the journal's copy of a day may
already hold entries written straight into it, so relocated ones are
merged into that order rather than appended after it.

Merged, not re-sorted: the entries already filed are never moved.
Re-sorting the whole day would silently rewrite journal history the
command was not asked to touch, and against real data the difference is
the whole safety margin -- relocating nine days of captures adds 824
lines and removes none.

An entry with no timestamp -- the end-of-day label carries properties
but no %U -- has nothing to be ordered by, so it comes to rest at the
end of its day rather than wherever it happened to be staged.

The journal is opened only when something is waiting, since opening it
is the cost staging exists to avoid, and it is saved before the capture
journal: should filing fail, the entries are still staged on disk and
the unsaved capture buffer can simply be reverted.

  each restated `"^\\*\\{%d\\} "'.

rather than from what they share.  Both need to visit a day's entries
and both need to know what "before" means, but neither concept was ever
lifted out of the first site that needed it -- the same shape the commit
that opened this branch removed one file over.

only code that knows an entry is a direct child of the datetree day, and
`agenda/journal--subtree-end' the only code that bounds a subtree; both
walks go through them.  `agenda/journal--entry-precedes-p' is the single
statement of the ordering rule, including what happens to an entry that
cannot be ordered, and `agenda/journal--file-day' now explains its
dated-first sort as a consequence of that rule rather than restating it.

subject: feat[emacs][kaizen]: log each command invocation as a minable event
message:
feat[emacs][kaizen]: log each command invocation as a minable event

[PROBLEM]
command-census reduces every invocation to a count at record time.
Counts rank commands for keybinding kaizen, but they destroy sequence,
timing and context -- exactly the dimensions where frictions hide (the
same commands always traveling together means a missing binding or
abstraction).  Usage cannot be mined, by me or an agent, for frictions
never consciously noticed.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
Aggregation at record time is lossy by design: the tally's hash bump
throws away when the command ran, which keys invoked it, and where.  No
artifact retains the invocation itself, so no later analysis can
recover patterns from the data.

[CHANGE]
Record the invocation itself alongside the tally.  The pre-command
recorder now also pushes an event plist -- :time (ISO-8601 with
milliseconds, local time, so plain grep slices the log by the user's
days), :command, :keys, :buffer, :mode -- onto an in-memory list; the
existing flush machinery (timer, kill-emacs, mode toggle) appends
pending events to a per-instance log, one readable form per line.  The
log inherits the package's shard-per-writer design: private file per
instance, nothing to lock.  A newline prefixed to each appended batch
isolates a crash's torn tail, so damage degrades to missing events,
never a dead log; the reader skips unreadable lines.  Pending events
clear only after a successful append, so a failed write (full disk)
costs nothing -- the next flush retries.  Event files take a distinct
extension (.events) so the tally aggregation cannot mistake them for
shards, and the one exclusion list governs both artifacts, keeping the
log minable rather than a keystroke transcript.  The tally is kept
rather than derived from events because the artifacts age differently:
counts are a compact lifetime aggregate, the log gets sliced and
eventually pruned -- and for the same reason command-census-reset keeps
deleting only the tally, never the log.
Alternative considered: epoch-float timestamps -- rejected because the
log's primary consumer greps it as text.

Verified: eleven new ERT tests pin the log's contract (context fidelity
through the real command loop, chronological append, exclusions,
torn-tail recovery, failed-flush durability, per-instance isolation,
aggregate invisibility, contention-freedom, off-means-off, and reset
sparing the log); all 9 layer suites pass and byte-compilation is
warning-free.

message:
fix[emacs][ai]: release indicator registrations on every exit path

[PROBLEM]
With counted indicator semantics, a start whose stop never runs
wedges `ai/llm-activity-indicator-active-count' above zero for the
rest of the session: every later request cycles N->N+1->N without
reaching 0, so the spinner never turns off. Real paths leak exactly
this way: the prompt-optimization flow signals between its start and
stop (unresolved prompt-id, or the user-error inside its patch
callback), and `gptel-request' can signal synchronously after
`cognition/send-request' registered. Under the replaced boolean a
leak self-healed at the next request's completion; the count made it
permanent.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
Start/stop pairing was coordinated purely by caller convention:
nothing in the structure tied a registration's release to its
request's lifecycle, so every non-happy exit path had to remember to
stop -- and three didn't. A request carrying a custom callback slot
also bypassed the default callback's stop entirely.

[CHANGE]
`ai/--start-llm-activity-indicator' now returns a one-shot release
closure: releasing is exactly-once by construction, so a site may
release from both an error handler and a completion callback without
double-decrementing (which would steal a concurrent request's
registration). Dispatch sites release on every exit path:
`cognition/make-callback' wraps the chosen callback -- custom or
default, the wrapper owns the lifecycle, closing the custom-callback
leak -- and releases on final states via unwind-protect;
`cognition/send-request' rolls the registration back and re-signals
when dispatch itself signals; the prompt-optimization flow releases
from its patch callback's unwind-protect and from a rollback around
its synchronous prefix. The rejected alternative -- bare per-site
condition-case around start/stop -- would keep the invariant
conventional and re-scatter with each new dispatch site; the token
gives it one home. No dispatch site calls the raw stop anymore, so a
stray direct stop consuming a live request's decrement is gone from
the codebase; the raw stop stays clamped at zero for direct callers.
The scaffolding suite (uncommitted at the owner's direction) adds
exactly-once-release and failed-dispatch-rollback scenarios; all six
scenarios and the full layer suite pass.

subject: fix[emacs][ai]: make the indicator release invariant structural
message:
fix[emacs][ai]: make the indicator release invariant structural

[PROBLEM]
Re-review showed "release on every exit path" still held only by
convention, and three path families broke it. (1) The lifecycle
wrapper released only on the streaming finals t/nil/abort; gptel
delivers a non-streaming success as one callback carrying the full
response string, so every successful request through a :stream nil
backend (the layer's OpenAI Responses backend is one) leaked its
registration and wedged the spinner permanently -- on the success
path. (2) The rollbacks used condition-case with an `error' handler,
which does not catch quit: C-g at the optimize flow's read-string
prompt (or during dispatch) leaked the registration. (3) The
optimize flow parks its release inside -patch-prompt's completion
callback, but -patch-prompt broke its own "callback runs with t or
nil" contract when op application or the file append signaled,
orphaning the release.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
"What counts as a final state" lived in two places that disagreed:
response processing treated a non-streaming string as final while
the wrapper's memq did not. The rollback idiom encoded "any
non-local exit" as "any `error'", missing quit. And -patch-prompt
enforced its callback contract per error path by convention -- two
paths honored it, two did not.

[CHANGE]
One home per invariant. `cognition/--response-final-p' is now the
single home of the final-state fact, shared by the lifecycle wrapper
and the response pcase, so they cannot drift apart again. Both
dispatch sites replace condition-case with unwind-protect plus a
handoff flag: ownership of the release transfers to the async
callback only when dispatch returns normally, and any non-local
exit -- signal or quit alike -- rolls back on the way out and keeps
propagating. -patch-prompt moves its completion callback into an
unwind-protect with a success flag, making the contract hold on
every handler exit instead of per path. Alongside: `release'
becomes a required parameter of make-callback (its optionality
guarded a caller that does not exist) and the vestigial
declare-function for the raw stop is dropped. The scaffolding suite
(uncommitted at the owner's direction) grew four scenarios --
non-streaming success releases, streaming chunks do not, quit rolls
back, patch callback runs on op failure -- each red before this
change; all ten pass, layer suites 9/9.

subject: fix[emacs][ai]: end indicator activity with the request, not its callback
message:
fix[emacs][ai]: end indicator activity with the request, not its callback

[PROBLEM]
Two ways a request ends still left the spinner wrong. A request that
finishes carrying no parsed response -- an HTTP 200 whose output is
reasoning-only, which the layer's non-streaming backends can return --
never reaches the response callback at all, so its registration was
never released and the spinner stayed on for the rest of the session.
In the other direction, `cognition/-patch-prompt' treated every
callback invocation as its result: with `gptel-include-reasoning'
enabled layer-wide, gptel delivers reasoning as an extra invocation
ahead of the response, so the handler tried to parse a
(reasoning . TEXT) cons as JSON, failed, and reported failure early --
releasing the optimize flow's registration and launching a replay
while the patch request was still in flight, then doing it again when
the real response arrived.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
Both follow from hanging end-of-request work off the response
callback, which is neither guaranteed to run nor guaranteed to run
once: gptel invokes it once per event and skips it entirely when
`(or response (not (member http-status (200 100))))' is nil. The
previous commit's release covered the callback's final states, which
is an enumeration of the ways a request can end -- and enumerations
miss cases.

[CHANGE]
Bind the registration to the request's state machine instead of its
callback. `cognition/--fsm-on-request-end' returns a gptel FSM whose
terminal transitions (DONE, ERRS, ABRT) run cleanup; the machine
always reaches one of them, however the request ends, so the class is
closed rather than enumerated. `cognition/send-request' releases
there and `cognition/make-callback' no longer takes a release at all,
which also removes the wrapper it needed. `cognition/-patch-prompt'
gets the same treatment from both sides: it acts only on the result
invocation (asking the shared `cognition/--response-final-p' rather
than assuming a single call), and its completion callback is a
one-shot closure the machine invokes with nil if no result ever
arrives -- so its documented contract now holds per request, which is
what callers parking cleanup in it assume. Scaffolding (uncommitted
at the owner's direction) grew four scenarios, each red before this
change: response-less completion releases, aborted request releases,
the reasoning invocation is not mistaken for the result, and the
patch completion runs when the response callback is skipped. Two
existing scenarios were simulating half a request -- driving the
callback but never ending the request as gptel always does -- and now
simulate both. Fourteen scenarios pass; layer suites 9/9, 58 tests.

subject: fix[emacs][ai]: skip the replay when the patch did not apply
message:
fix[emacs][ai]: skip the replay when the patch did not apply

[PROBLEM]
A failed patch now launches a replay. `cognition/-patch-prompt' was
just made to report every outcome, including the failures that
previously went unreported -- a response-less completion, an op that
would not apply, a file append that signalled. Its only caller binds
that outcome as `ok' and never reads it, so the optimize flow treats
"the patch failed" exactly like "the patch applied": it spends a real
LLM request replaying the UNPATCHED prompt, then runs a differential
diagnosis comparing that trace against the original -- a diff of a
prompt against itself.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
Widening a contract changes what its consumers must handle. The
callback could previously ignore `ok' without visible harm, because
the paths that would have passed nil never called it at all; making
the contract total turned a latent omission into reachable behavior.
The caller was not revisited when the contract moved.

[CHANGE]
Honour the outcome: the flow replays only when the patch applied, and
otherwise reports that it is skipping the replay. The registration is
released either way, by the unwind form that already owned it.
Scaffolding (uncommitted at the owner's direction) grew both
directions of the branch -- a failed patch does not replay and does

fix[emacs][ai]: refuse to dispatch when gptel's terminal states move

[PROBLEM]
The indicator's cleanup is appended to gptel's DONE, ERRS and ABRT
state handlers by name. gptel calls the state machine "an unstable
feature and subject to change", and appending to a state that no
longer exists is a silent no-op: an upstream rename would leave every
request without cleanup, the count wedged above zero, and the spinner
on for the rest of the session. That is precisely the failure this
indirection was introduced to eliminate, reachable again through a
dependency seam and with no signal that anything went wrong.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The terminal states are a fact about a dependency, restated here as a
literal. Restating a fact is safe only when a drift is noticed;
`mapcar' over an alist notices nothing, so the copy could go stale
silently.

[CHANGE]
Check the states exist before wiring cleanup to them, and signal when
one does not. The failure then surfaces where it can be understood --
at dispatch, naming the missing state -- and `with-activity-registration'
rolls the registration back on the way out, so a broken seam costs an
error message rather than a spinner nobody can turn off. Scaffolding
(uncommitted at the owner's direction) grew a scenario simulating an
upstream rename: it asserts both that the failure is raised and that
no registration survives it, red before this change. Seventeen
scenarios pass; layer suites 9/9, 58 tests.

message:
feat[dotfiles][emacs/technical-writing]: toggle M-q between fill and unfill by text state

[PROBLEM]
Unfilling a paragraph needs its own chord: M-q always fills, and only
C-u M-q unfills. The prefix makes the writer state a fact the buffer
already knows -- whether the text is currently wrapped.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
technical-writing/org-fill-or-unfill-paragraph encoded the operation's
direction in the keypress (the UNFILL prefix argument) instead of in
the text. Wrapped and unwrapped text each admit only one useful fill
operation, so the prefix carried no information the target paragraph's
shape does not already determine.

[CHANGE]
M-q now reads the direction from its target: a paragraph (or active
region) spanning multiple lines unfills into single logical lines;
anything else fills to fill-column. Wrapped is detected as two adjacent
non-blank lines, so a ragged mid-edit paragraph unfills instead of
re-filling, and blank separators keep a neighboring paragraph's shape
out of the verdict. fill-paragraph is called directly rather than via
call-interactively so a stale C-u cannot leak in as JUSTIFY='full.
The rejected alternative, a last-command repeat toggle (the
unfill-toggle idiom), fills first regardless of state and only unfills
on the second press -- still modal, merely modal in time. The new
fill-or-unfill-test.el suite pins the contract: both toggle directions,
the ragged case, paragraph-at-point scope, and region scope.

to unwrap, so fill normally. Verdict and action are now the same
fill-paragraph call on the same text by construction; no code
re-derives bounds, so there is nothing left to drift out of sync.

[PROBLEM]
Real use surfaced the wrong reading of "wrapped": editing a filled
paragraph leaves it ragged, and M-q unwrapped that work in progress
instead of re-tidying it. The suite pinned this on purpose -- the
literal spec said wrapped text unwraps -- but the report shows the
intended model: M-q should always do the useful thing, and unfilling a
paragraph the writer is mid-edit on is not it.

workable definition is operational (filling would change nothing).
Under the structural reading the most common M-q scenario -- tidy the
paragraph I just edited -- became the one case the key got wrong.

nothing unfill. Ragged text re-fills in one press, canonical text
unfills, a too-long line wraps, a fitting line stays put; the mixed
region consequently normalizes to filled (the tidying direction) --
respecified in the suite alongside the ragged case.

The change detector also had to change: a fill of canonical text
deletes and re-inserts identical line breaks, so the O(1) modified
tick reads byte-identical rewrites as change (the direction-swapped
twin of the caveat on the tick commit -- the suite's unfill tests
caught it). Text comparison returns, scoped O(target) rather than
O(buffer): the span comes from the same use-region-p and
org-element-at-point oracles org-fill-paragraph itself consults, so it
scopes the comparison without re-deriving the fill's target -- the
coupling removed two rounds ago stays removed, and a keypress in a

Review of #319 found four defects: (1) the crisis stand-down branch was
dead code — "crisis" can never come out of a require-match completing-read
over dsq-intents, which does not contain it, so a crisis day faced the
full item battery; (2) even if reachable, the branch was skipped on the
full form while the canonical note specifies an unconditional stand-down;
(3) the note and dsq.el restate three sets of behavior-determining facts
(reverse flags, core probes, vocabularies) with no mechanical link — one
drifted reverse flag silently inverts a dimension for every future day;
(4) dsq-version "2" and the note's "v1.0" gave one instrument two
unrelated version identities.

The stand-down was modeled as an INTENT, but a crisis is never intended —
so its value was left out of the intent vocabulary and the guard compared
against a member that could not exist; the form-conditional guard then
compounded the mismatch. The duplication and the version split are the
same failure at the artifact level: facts coordinated by value between
the note and the code, with nothing that fails when they disagree — the
dead "crisis" literal was that convention's first casualty.

offers dsq-standdown-option ("crisis_standdown") alongside the true
intents and short-circuits — unconditionally, on both forms — to a
presence-only entry (archetype "crisis", optional one-liner). Unify the
version: dsq-version "1" stamps the note's major, and both bump together
by documented contract. Make the note<->code agreement mechanical where a
runtime link is not worth its weight: two new ert tests parse the
canonical note and assert its (R) flags, star probes, intent/archetype/
modifier vocabularies, stand-down option, and version stamp against this
package's constants — drift now fails the suite instead of shipping. Two
further tests pin stand-down reachability on both forms (mocked reads)
and the presence-only drawer shape. Alternative considered: generating

feat[dsq]: v2.0 — compress to 14 yes/no questions across 6 transferable dimensions

[PROBLEM]
Owner review of the v1 instrument (PR #319): a 25-item 1-5 Likert battery
is a formal psychometric instrument, too expensive to fill nightly;
number scales are unwanted; several items leak era-specific phrasing
(price-checking, dancing/craft exemplars) so the dimensions overfit
phases of this one life. The request: the minimal set of transferable
dimensions that still represents the majority of days, captured with 2-3
yes/no questions each, cheap enough to breeze through while keeping
enough fidelity to classify and traverse days by profile.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
v1 optimized for measurement fidelity per-day (REQ-style Likert
redundancy, diagnostics, intent anchor, archetype picker) and paid for it
in nightly cost and person-specific wording; the corpus evidence properly
justified WHICH constructs matter, but v1 also let the corpus dictate
item wording and auxiliary machinery, coupling the instrument to the
current era and to the author's vocabulary.

[CHANGE]
v2.0: 6 dimensions (MOMENTUM, COMMAND, FOCUS, RECHARGE, BODY, FUEL) x
2-3 yes/no questions + one global = 14 keypresses, ~30 seconds. The
corpus decides which dimensions exist (minimality: every candidate merge
collapses a day-type pair the corpus distinguishes); wording is
era-free and transferable (nurse/student/retiree test). Classification
now EMERGES from the profile — the archetype picker, intent anchor,
modifiers, crisis stand-down, and core/full cadence split are all
removed (14 cheap bits need no gating). FOCUS carries three separate
failure bits (external pull, own loops, scatter) that are never summed
away — the bits are the diagnosis, and the scatter question restores
the fragmentation-as-depletion signal the corpus flagged. An
adversarial critique of the draft binary form drove six wording fixes
(felt-restfulness vs work-absence, wanted-outcome vs procedural choice,
de-inflated global, de-branded external pull). Every v2 question
descends from a v1 item that survived the 36-day blind-rater study;
dsq-version bumps to "2" per the versioning contract, and the ert
suite's note<->code tests now enforce codes, good-pole keying, the
2-3-questions rule, and the version stamp. The v1 long form is archived

subject: fix[emacs][hydra]: quit any hydra with C-] via a base-map head
message:
fix[emacs][hydra]: quit any hydra with C-] via a base-map head

[PROBLEM]
The cognition-tools menu (M-t) traps you. Pressing C-] to leave does
nothing but echo "An amaranth Hydra can only exit through a blue head"
over and over; only `q`, a tool key, or C-g get you out.

[ROOT-CAUSE]
The generated cognition-tools body sets `:foreign-keys warn`. On every
keypress hydra's `hydra--clearfun` intercepts any key that is not one of
the body's own heads, rebinds it to `hydra-amaranth-warn`, and keeps the
map active -- so C-] (`abort-recursive-edit'), an ordinary foreign key,
warns instead of quitting. C-g escapes only because clearfun
special-cases `keyboard-quit'. Nothing ever wired C-] in.

[CHANGE]
Bind C-] to `hydra-keyboard-quit' in `hydra-base-map' -- the keymap every
hydra copies at definition time -- so the key becomes a genuine head that
beats the warn branch and quits cleanly in every hydra, with no per-hydra
edits. The binding lives in kaizen's pretty-hydra `:config', which runs
before the hydras (and the lazily-built cognition-tools menu) copy the
base map. The deliberate lock stays intact: only the conventional abort
key gains passage; stray keys still warn. The binding is extracted as a
pure keymap transformation (`kaizen/--hydra-bind-abort-key') so a test
pins the outcome on a throwaway map.

Alternatives considered: dropping `:foreign-keys warn' would make
cognition-tools consistent with the other hydras but removes the
intentional lock and leaves C-] running `abort-recursive-edit' -> a
spurious "No recursive edit is in progress" error; adding an explicit
head in the generator fixes only this one hydra and is exactly the
per-hydra patching this avoids.

subject: fix[emacs][kaizen]: defer elfeed instead of loading it at startup
message:
fix[emacs][kaizen]: defer elfeed instead of loading it at startup

[PROBLEM]
Every Emacs launch reports "Error (use-package): elfeed/:catch: End of
file during parsing: #<killed buffer>" in the warnings buffer, and
elfeed plus its whole dependency chain (elfeed-goodies, powerline,
popwin, ...) load during startup even though the Spacemacs elfeed
layer declares the package deferred until first use (SPC a r e).

[CAUSE]
kaizen/post-init-elfeed's use-package form had :config but no :defer.
Spacemacs leaves use-package-always-defer nil, so the form require'd
elfeed on the spot at every startup, overriding the layer's :defer t.
That eager require walks elfeed's load chain, and a broken file in the
chain aborts the Lisp reader mid-form; recent Emacs signals
end-of-file with the reader's temporary load buffer (killed on unwind)
as the error data, which use-package's :catch renders as the
killed-buffer warning at startup instead of at first elfeed use.

[CHANGE]
Add :defer t so the form registers configuration without loading the
package; the setq moves into the :config block that runs once elfeed
actually loads. Verified in batch Emacs against the real elfeed
source: post-init leaves elfeed unloaded, and the feed list is in
effect after (require 'elfeed). A throwaway ERT suite demonstrated the
defect red/green during development and is intentionally left
uncommitted.

The second field run cleared the emacs build (host nix realized

cd/pwd after creation. Pinned by a new expectation that stubs
nix-build/nix-store/docker on PATH, invokes the script by relative path
with a relative EMACS_CACHE_OUT, and asserts every recorded -v host
side is absolute — red against the old code with exactly the two

fix[agents][devenv]: bundle the emacs-lightning site packages into the devenv emacs

tmrts layer dependencies) and died at coding/funcs.el:94: a top-level
(require 'vterm) — "Cannot open load file: vterm". The batch package
install aborts before installing anything.

hard-requires them. The devenv shipped the bare emacs-git base, so the

error rather than a silent regression to bare emacs.
